subject: iot
title: Unit 4 — TinyML, Time-Series & Predictive Maintenance MCQs

options: Training huge models in the cloud
Running ML inference on microcontrollers / ultra-low-power constrained devices (KB of memory, mW of power)
items.explain: TinyML runs ML inference directly on microcontrollers — pushing intelligence to the edge for low latency, offline operation, bandwidth savings, privacy, and power efficiency.

items.q: In a TinyML workflow, where do training and inference happen?
options: Training in the cloud (heavy); only inference on the device
Training on the device, inference in the cloud
items.explain: Training is heavy and data-hungry, done in the cloud (TensorFlow/PyTorch). Only the finished, compressed model runs inference on the MCU — you never train on the microcontroller.

items.q: Which technique shrinks a model (e.g., 32-bit floats → 8-bit integers) so it fits on a microcontroller?
items.explain: Quantization reduces weight precision (e.g., to 8-bit ints), shrinking model size and speeding inference with usually small accuracy loss — key to fitting models in KB of memory.

items.q: A benefit of TinyML over cloud inference is:
options: It ships only the result (e.g., 'keyword detected'), giving low latency, offline operation, bandwidth savings, and privacy
It needs a data center on the device
items.explain: By inferring on-device, TinyML sends conclusions not raw data — fast, works offline, saves bandwidth, and keeps raw data (voice/images) private. Tools include TensorFlow Lite for Microcontrollers and Edge Impulse.

items.q: Why is a time-series database (e.g., InfluxDB) preferred over a relational DB for IoT telemetry?
options: It enforces complex joins between entities
It is optimized for high-rate timestamped writes, native time-range aggregation, and retention/downsampling
items.explain: TSDBs specialize in the (timestamp, value, tags) shape: fast high-volume writes, native 'average per interval' queries, and built-in retention/downsampling to keep years of history cheap.

items.q: What is Grafana's role in the IoT stack?
options: It stores raw sensor data permanently
It visualizes time-series data as live dashboards and fires alerts when metrics cross thresholds
items.explain: Grafana reads from data sources like InfluxDB to build real-time, auto-refreshing dashboards and to alert (email/Slack/webhook) on threshold breaches — implementing the pipeline's visualization + action stages.

items.q: The classic open-source IoT monitoring pairing is:
items.explain: InfluxDB is the memory (time-series store); Grafana is the eyes (live dashboards + alerting). Devices write to InfluxDB; Grafana reads it back as charts and alerts.

items.q: What does 'downsampling' (retention) in a time-series DB achieve?
options: Keeps recent raw data but stores only summaries (e.g., hourly averages) long-term, keeping years of history affordable
Increases the sampling rate of sensors
items.explain: Downsampling stores high-resolution data short-term and aggregated summaries long-term (e.g., raw for a day, hourly averages forever), controlling storage cost while preserving trends.

items.q: Why is predictive maintenance superior to reactive and preventive maintenance?
options: It fixes equipment exactly when sensor data indicates need — avoiding both unplanned breakdowns and unnecessary early servicing
It schedules repairs on a fixed calendar
It only fixes machines after they fail
items.explain: Reactive fixes after failure (downtime); preventive fixes on a calendar (often too early/late); predictive uses live data to act at the optimal moment — the cost/safety sweet spot.

items.q: Which ML technique predicts the Remaining Useful Life (RUL) of a component?
items.explain: RUL ('~12 days left') is a continuous value, so it's a regression task. Anomaly detection flags abnormal readings; classification labels states (healthy/degrading/faulty).

items.q: Which sensor signals are most commonly used for predictive maintenance of machinery?
options: Vibration, temperature, current, and acoustic data
items.explain: Vibration, temperature, current, acoustic, and oil-quality signals reveal mechanical degradation (e.g., a failing bearing) — fed to ML to forecast failure before it happens.

items.q: A key ML challenge specific to predictive maintenance is:
options: Data imbalance — failures are rare, so there are few positive examples to learn from (plus model drift over time)
items.explain: Failures are rare, creating class imbalance (few positive examples). Combined with model drift (sensor behavior changing), this makes training robust predictive models challenging — addressed via the feedback loop.
